snippet.title: What to do if you live in the path of a volcano - Arianna Soldati
snippet.description:
Explore 3 strategies to control the flow of lava, and how scientists are using them to protect communities from future eruptions.

--

In December 2023, Icelandic citizens experienced their worst nightmare: a volcanic fissure opened and began spewing lava fountains 100 meters tall. While the molten rock narrowly avoided a small town, Iceland wasn’t willing to leave anyone's fate to chance again and began preparing for future eruptions. Arianna Soldati explores 3 potential strategies to control these red-hot rivers of destruction.

snippet.description:
Deep beneath southern Norway, scientists have just confirmed the staggering discovery of a massive rare earth deposit at the Fen site holding a game-changing 15.9 million metric tons of critical minerals. As Europe's absolute largest reserve—seven times bigger than any other—this colossal underground treasure is set to completely reshape global supply chains and break the world's heavy reliance on foreign monopolies. An incredible twenty percent of this monumental find consists of highly prized neodymium and praseodymium, the exact super-metals required to power next-generation electric vehicle motors, massive wind turbines, and cutting-edge military hardware. Mining operations are actively fast-tracking to extract these crucial elements, fueling the ultimate green energy transition and triggering a massive new European industrial boom. snippet.title: This Rare Brain Trait Makes You Feel Other People’s Pain 🧠
snippet.description:
Did you know that some people feel pain just by seeing it?

Less than 2% of people experience something called mirror-touch synesthesia.

People with mirror-touch synesthesia don’t just see what happens to others - they physically feel it.

If they watch someone get tapped on the arm,
they may feel a tap on their own arm.

If they see someone get hurt,
they can feel pain in the same location on their own body.

It’s like a weird superpower and researchers have found that mirror-touch synesthesia appears more often in people whose work involves deep social understanding like actors, therapists, and caregivers.

Around 2 to 3% of people have something called face blindness, or prosopagnosia.

Face blindness doesn’t mean poor eyesight.
It means the brain can’t recognize faces - even familiar ones.

Imagine not recognizing coworkers, close friends…
or even members of your own family.

In severe cases, someone with face blindness can look in a mirror and feel like they’re seeing a stranger.

So how do they recognize people?

They rely on context and clues instead of faces.
Things like voice, hairstyle, clothing, posture, or where they expect to see someone.

Someone with face blindness might recognize their partner by the way they walk.

Or recognize a coworker only at the office, but not at the grocery store.

snippet.title: How did ancient civilizations brew beer? - Malcolm Purinton
snippet.description:
Trace the history and evolution of beer, from its first known existence 13,000 years ago to the modern beverage we know today.

--

Today, there are over 100 distinct beer varieties, from pilsners and bocks, to porters, stouts, and IPAs. The oldest evidence of beer brewing dates back 13,000 years, but experts believe the drink developed independently across the world. So, how did ancient civilizations brew beer, and how did their methods develop into the beverage we know today? Malcolm Purinton traces the evolution of beer.

Lesson Malcolm Purinton, directed by Anton Bogaty.

snippet.title: The Girl Who Fell From The Sky 🪂❌
snippet.description:
So this teenage girl fell two miles through the sky still strapped to her seat… but the fall wasn’t even the worst part.

On Christmas Eve 1971, 17 year old Juliane Koepcke boarded LANSA Flight 508 with her mother - but 25 minutes into the flight, lightning struck the plane, and caused it to explode mid-air.

Juliane was thrown out, and dropped 10,000 feet. 
She passed out mid air and next morning, she woke up alone in the amazon jungle.

Her mother… and all 90 other passengers… were gone.
She had a fractured collarbone, and a deep cut on her leg.

But her father had once told that if she was ever lost in the rainforest - she needed to find a river and follow it downstream.

So for days she pushed forward: fighting hunger, thirst, and maggot infested wounds.

Against all odds on the 11th day, exhausted and barely conscious, Juliane somehow stumbled into a group of loggers who rushed her to safety.

snippet.title: The Wolves That Live Off The Ocean 🐟🐺
snippet.description:
Did you know that sea wolves are a real thing?

The term “sea wolf” refers to a subspecies of grey wolf found on the Canadian West coast. 

You see, regular wolves depend on large prey like elk and deer. But as human development pushed these wolves closer to the shoreline, they were forced to adapt.

Sea wolves survive on a diet that’s up to 80% seafood - including salmon, seals, and even sea otters. Amazingly, they’re also smart enough to avoid eating the otter’s livers, which contain dangerously high levels of shellfish toxin.

And because their food is smaller, and more scattered sea wolves have evolved to be about 20% smaller than their inland cousins.
